answer.rationale: The line is running at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, so any move that introduces delivery-risk uncertainty (like switching to an unproven low-cost vendor at full volume) could be catastrophic even if it meets the 18% cost mandate on paper — memory_c2's quick onboarding and clean invoicing say nothing about sustained on-time delivery at scale or quality consistency under stress, which is the real risk given no buffer. In contrast, memory_c4 shows that benchmarking and renegotiating with the incumbent at renewal has previously recovered real margin on both price and payment terms without any migration risk or service disruption, and memory_c6 confirms the incumbent has flexed on price via longer-term commitments without narrowing scope. Given the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, the fastest path to meaningful cost reduction without jeopardizing delivery continuity is to aggressively renegotiate with the incumbent using the low-cost quote as leverage, rather than committing the full primary volume to an unvetted vendor under zero-slack conditions. I verified memory_c4 to confirm the renegotiation outcome was a real, durable margin recovery and not a one-time or reversed concession, since that's the load-bearing assumption for this action. This does not fully resolve whether negotiation alone can hit the full 18% target — that residual gap and the unvalidated low-cost vendor reliability are explicitly flagged as downstream risks for the next review cycle rather than resolved here.
